tagline: Fjords, northern lights, and midnight sun
overview:
Norway runs up the western edge of Scandinavia in a long, narrow strip, its coastline so chewed by fjords and islands that, measured around every inlet, it stretches for tens of thousands of kilometers. The country is slightly larger than New Mexico, reaches far above the Arctic Circle, and shares land borders with Sweden, Finland, and Russia.

About 5.5 million people live in Norway, most of them in the south near Oslo, the capital at the head of a long fjord. Norwegian has two written forms, Bokmål and Nynorsk, and Sami languages are spoken by the Indigenous Sami people of the north. Norway is a constitutional monarchy with a king and an elected parliament called the Storting.

Oil and gas found under the North Sea in the 1960s made Norway wealthy, and the government saves much of that money in a fund meant for future generations. Almost all the country's electricity comes from water rushing down mountains through hydropower stations.
landAndNature: Glaciers of the last ice age gouged Norway's fjords, long sea inlets with cliffs dropping straight into deep water; Sognefjord reaches more than 200 kilometers inland. Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier on mainland Europe, and Galdhøpiggen, the highest peak, stands 2,469 meters tall. North of the Arctic Circle the sun never sets for weeks in summer and never rises for weeks in winter, when the aurora borealis ripples green across the sky. The Gulf Stream keeps the coast surprisingly mild and ice-free. Puffins, sea eagles, and millions of seabirds nest on cliff ledges, while reindeer, moose, arctic foxes, and lemmings live inland and musk oxen graze the Dovrefjell plateau.
peopleAndCulture: Norwegians spend time outdoors in every season, an idea they call friluftsliv, or open-air living, and children play outside in snow and rain from nursery age. Skiing began here, and Norway has won more Winter Olympic medals than any other country; cross-country skiing, biathlon, and ski jumping are followed the way soccer is elsewhere. The food leans on the sea: salmon, cod dried into stockfish, pickled herring, along with brown cheese, waffles, and open sandwiches. Constitution Day on May 17 fills the streets with children's parades and national costumes called bunads. The Sami herd reindeer and have their own parliament and flag.
history: Hunters followed the retreating ice into Norway roughly 11,000 years ago. From about 793, Norse seafarers known as the Vikings raided and traded across Europe, settled Iceland and Greenland, and reached North America around the year 1000, where Leif Erikson landed in a place he called Vinland. Harald Fairhair united much of Norway in the late 800s, and Christianity arrived soon after. Plague and politics left Norway under Danish rule for four centuries, then Swedish rule after 1814, the year it wrote its constitution. Full independence came peacefully in 1905. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945, and resistance fighters sabotaged a plant making heavy water for German research. Oil found in 1969 transformed the economy.
funFacts: Measured around every fjord and island, Norway's coastline runs roughly 100,000 kilometers, more than twice the distance around the equator.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded each December in Oslo, the only Nobel prize not handed out in Sweden.
A king penguin at Edinburgh Zoo named Nils Olav is an honorary member of Norway's King's Guard and has been knighted.
In the town of Rjukan, giant mirrors on a mountainside bounce winter sunlight into the square, which otherwise sits in shadow for months.
Salmon sushi was largely a Norwegian idea, promoted in Japan during the 1980s to sell farmed Atlantic salmon.
